 Cultura Geek

Monster Hunter: Wilds represents the natural evolution of the franchise, introducing a series of improvements and, above all, quality-of-life features that make it more accessible to all kinds of players. It's a title that notably changes the traditional structure of separate missions and hunting zones, opting instead for an open world featuring distinct ecosystems and areas filled with a vast number of monsters to hunt. These enhancements don't stray far from the series' original formula, although they do make playing Monster Hunter somewhat easier and less frustrating.

Monster Hunter Wilds delivers a ton of incredible new content, buried underneath the usual UI nightmare plus a long, interminable campaign. The new features of the game are fun and exciting once the game opens up, and there are a ton of awesome new monsters to battle. The graphics, as always, are stunning. But wading through the mud of this story for 15-20 hours is downright painful, and the franchise's tradition of not explaining itself is getting extremely old. There is a fabulous Monster Hunter game here, but sooner or later this franchise is going to have to wake up to the need to wipe the slate clean and open the doors for new players. Instead, Monster Hunter Wilds feels like it is going in the other direction.

The problem when reviewing a game of this scale, part of a series with more than ten entries, is that personal attachment and nostalgia inevitably play a crucial role. It’s clear that the franchise no longer offers the same experience as it did years ago. The rough, unwelcoming, and flamboyant feel of the past has given way to unwavering accessibility, a clear pursuit of simplicity, and a deliberate openness to newcomers. While the game’s addictive foundations are still present, they are nonetheless hindered by an at times excessive simplification of its mechanics. However, Monster Hunter Wilds remains a thrilling experience, even for veterans—provided they accept that it is no longer the game they once knew.

results.title: Nintendo Switch 2 Is Finally Getting Capcom’s Fastest-Selling Game Ever
results.author: Jen Glennon
highlights:
By Jen Glennon 

 Published Nov 15, 2026, 2:00 PM EST 

# Nintendo Switch 2 is finally getting Capcom’s fastest-selling game ever

Image: Capcom

With the success of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, it's safe to say that Capcom has had a fantastic 2026. And the venerable developer's 2025 wasn't too shabby either. Last February, it released Monster Hunter Wilds for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. It went on to sell a whopping eight million copies in just three days, making it the company's fastest-selling game of all time. As of September 2026, Monster Hunter Wilds has sold 12.2 million copies, making it Capcom's 11th-best-selling game of all time. That number is set to go up significantly after Dec. 4, when it finally launches for Nintendo Switch 2.

Monster Hunter Wilds is the first game in the series to let players bring two weapons into the field — you can swap your loadout on the go thanks to your helpful bird friend known as a Seikret. It also adds pop-up camps to allow for a more seamless experience with less backtracking. The new wound system allows players to target a beast's weak points and dole out even bigger damage. You can play with couch co-op, or online with up to three buddies. Best of all, it doesn't matter which console they have — Monster Hunter Wilds supports cross-platform play between all versions, including Nintendo Switch 2,

Folks who pre-order the game ahead of the Dec. 4 launch, will also get a substantial discount. Through Dec. 3, Monster Hunter Wilds is on sale through the Nintendo eShop for $29.99, a 25% discount from its MSRP of $39.99. If you want to try before you buy, there's also a demo featuring the game's prologue available now on all platforms. Save data from the demo will transfer over to the full game if you decide to make a purchase.

...

If you're a die-hard Monster Hunter fan, the Gold Edition includes an extensive collection of more than 170 DLC cosmetics to customize your character. The Gold Edition isn't currently on sale, and retails for $79.99. That said, the DLC bundle on its own retails for a cool $59.99, so The Gold Edition is slightly cheaper than purchasing the DLC later.

Capcom also has big plans for Monster Hunter Wilds in 2027. The upcoming Ascendance DLC is billed by Capcom as a "massive expansion," which will add a new location called the Skybound Eyrie, which is a network of ancient floating island ruins. It will also introduce challenging Master Rank quests and new monster types. Back in February, series director Ryōzō Tsujimoto said Ascendance will be comparable in scope to previous paid expansions, like Monster Hunter World's massive Iceborne DLC.

results.title: Monster Hunter Wilds news, guides, and updates | PC Gamer
results.author: Lincoln Carpenter
highlights:
Monster Hunter Wilds has "entered the area," as it would say of one of its giant roaring enemies storming onto the scene. Far from an unbeatable monstrosity though, Wilds is the best starting point yet for the long-running series with its open world, streamlined combat systems, and slightly less clunky co-op system than past games. (Slightly).

Capcom has been in the monster slaying biz for a long time, as have Monster Hunter fans, so expectations and opinions around how it plays to the series formula are plenty varied. Our Monster Hunter Wilds review calls it "best in class monster combat," but also notes it has "a wilderness that's a touch too streamlined," compared to series history. But we have so, so much more to say about it, and a mountain of advice on how to smoothly ascend through the ranks of the Hunter's Guild.
